Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities  
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
 
v.  
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
AD24-11-000 
 
 
EL25-20-000 
(Consolidated) 
 
 
 
 
 
ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDING UNDER SECTION 206 OF THE FEDERAL POWER 
ACT AND CONSOLIDATING WITH OTHER PROCEEDINGS 
 
COMMENTS OF THE UNION OF CONCERNED SCIENTISTS 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, the Union of Concerned Scientists 
(“UCS”), respectfully submits these comments in support of the filings dated March 24, 2025 of 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, and Public 
Service Gas & Electric made in response to Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order Instituting 
Proceeding under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other 
Proceedings (the “Show Cause Order”).1  In these filings, these utilities base their conclusions 
and recommendations on the fact that large loads connecting to existing generation are 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025).

synchronized to the transmission system, use the transmission system, and rely on the 
transmission system. UCS provides support for this set of assertions. 
The Union of Concerned Scientists is a national nonprofit organization that has been 
participating in PJM stakeholder processes and Commission dockets for over 10 years, 
representing our members and the public interest in advancing responsible public policies in 
areas where science and technologies play a critical role. Established in 1969, UCS has created a 
unique alliance between many of the nation’s leading scientists and thousands of committed 
citizens. The UCS Climate & Energy Program focuses on developing a sustainable energy 
system—one that is affordable and nondepletable, and that does not degrade natural systems or 
public health. UCS is headquartered in Cambridge, MA and has offices in Berkeley, CA, 
Chicago, IL and Washington, D.C. 
UCS thanks the Commission for initiating this inquiry and consolidating the disparate 
proceedings that have examined filings that sought to inappropriately narrow the scope for 
Commission review. The swift and proper resolution of the central questions in this inquiry will 
protect consumers from costs and society from substantial reliability risks that have not been 
seen or addressed in the past. 
I. 
INTRODUCTION 
These comments support PJM’s conclusion that  “all co-located load be served from the 
PJM Transmission System as PJM Network Load with applicable firm transmission service.”2  
UCS also supports the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners view that “consider all the 
arrangements being contemplated or requested as being interconnected with and synchronized 
 
2 Show Cause Order para 4, citing PJM Guidance on Co-Located Load (March 22, 2024).

with the transmission and/or distribution grid and thus not “fully isolated.”3 Lastly, UCS supports 
Public Service Gas & Electric assertion that co-located loads “use or impact the transmission.”4 
 While UCS makes these comments with a focus on data centers, which are sufficiently 
common to establish experience in the utility sector and are also the overwhelming majority of 
new large loads proposed in PJM, the same conclusions should be applied to any large 
homogeneous new load added to a generator interconnection. 
Reliance on a single generator exclusively to serve loads and addition of loads in size 
range of 100 MW to 1,000 MW are practices generally not seen in the U.S. power system since 
the bulk power system allowed consolidation of utility company service territories and the 
synchronization of multiple generators to serve interconnected loads more than a century ago. 
The Commission should reject the proposition that loads of this size will be synchronized and yet 
have no clarity as to how they interact with the regulated power system. Under the proposed 
arrangements that claim “fully isolated”, there would be no planning or capacity to serve the load 
in the event of the closure of the host generator. In such an event, the system will have two holes 
to fill, one from the retirement of the generator and the other due to the appearance of the load 
suddenly ready and willing to take service from the network.5 As a threshold matter, the claim 
these loads are “fully isolated” is refuted by their normal operation requiring system generation 
 
3 Answer of the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to the Order Instituting the Proceeding 
Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other Proceedings (“TO 
filing”) at page 9. 
4 Response of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to the Order to Show Cause at page 14. 
5  See Technical Conference Transcript (Bresler) at 40:11-21 (“[C]an I really plan the system on 
that basis? In other words, if that generator is unavailable,” given “the potential criticality of the 
loads that we are talking about,” then “[i]s it going to be an acceptable answer” to not serve that 
load based on its contractual commitments “to not be on the system if that generator is 
unavailable”?)

reserves and transmission capacity when the output of the co-located generator does not match 
their consumption.  
Because the operation of a data center is not supported solely by a single generator, the 
premise that there isn’t electricity from the grid flowing to the data center is simply unsupported 
and false. There may be a contract, but the laws of physics and the observed behavior of 
numerous data centers refute the claim that electrical separation is accomplished by placing the 
generator and load behind a single meter and observing that “the load is not receiving electricity 
from the grid.” In short, there is Network Load, requiring Network Integrated Transmission 
Service (or Point-to-Point Service), and Ancillary Services, in all the proposed configurations. 
 
II. 
BACKGROUND 
The construction and operation of data centers in the U.S. has doubled in the past four to five 
years.6 Developers of data centers, as well as other large loads and fleet electrification facilities, 
have experienced delays, constraints and expense due to the limited physical capacity of both 
transmission and distribution systems around the country. The constraining nature of existing 
infrastructure and the costs to plan and construct new transmission and distribution capability is 
not unique to data centers, new loads or even the electric power industry.7  
 
6 Hyperscale Data Center Count Hits 1,136; Average Size Increases; US Accounts for 54% of 
Total Capacity. Synergy Research Group. March 19, 2025 
https://www.srgresearch.com/articles/hyperscale-data-center-count-hits-1136-average-size-
increases-us-accounts-for-54-of-total-capacity  
7 Delays in generation interconnection on both distribution and transmission circuits are more 
visible than delays attaching load. However, they are similar, requiring similar equipment and 
coordination with the same entities. See for example Rand, Joseph, Nick Manderlink, Will 
Gorman, Ryan H Wiser, Joachim Seel, Julie Mulvaney Kemp, Seongeun Jeong, and Fritz 
Kahrl."Queued Up: 2024 Edition, Characteristics of Power Plants Seeking Transmission 
Interconnection As of the End of 2023." (2024).

In recent months the Commission has opened six dockets relating to the treatment and cost 
allocation of large loads co-located, i.e. interconnected on the generation side of a generator’s 
point of interconnection. This debate about the services required first appeared at the 
Commission as a modification of an existing generator’s interconnection agreement. In 
November 2024, the Commission rejected one FPA Section 205 filing that sets forth a proposal 
under which the “fully isolated co-located load” would have paid no transmission or ancillary 
charges.8 Also in November, Constellation Energy Generation, LLC (Constellation) filed a 
complaint against PJM in Docket No. EL25-20-000. Constellation argues that the PJM Open 
Access Transmission Tariff (OATT) is unjust, unreasonable and unduly discriminatory because it 
does not contain rules for interconnected generators to follow when seeking to serve a co-located 
load configuration that Constellation argues is fully isolated from the grid.9  Constellation builds 
its argument on the premise that it can provide service to end-use load co-located behind the 
meter in a configuration with protective relays to prevent the load from receiving electricity from 
the grid, a configuration that Constellation refers to as “Fully Isolated Co-Located Load.”10  
In response to the Constellation complaint, several parties dispute Constellation’s 
characterization of “Fully Isolated Co-Located Load” and argue that the arrangement requires 
wholesale services.11 In addition, load-serving entities argue that PJM’s transmission rates are 
 
8 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 189 FERC ¶ 61,078 (2024) (rejecting the amended ISA for failing 
to meet the requisite burden of proof).   
9 Show Cause Order para 1. 
10 Id. para 50. 
11 “PJM argues that grid-connected resources and load cannot follow only certain electrons along 
a contract path. NOVEC states that the Guidance Document provides that co-located load 
“benefits from the use of the Transmission System and Ancillary Services.” Exelon argues that a 
nuclear facility serving co-located load must remain interconnected to the grid. Several parties 
argue that the arrangement relies upon services from the grid, such as load following, voltage 
support, black start, uplift, backup power, and certain ancillary services, because a nuclear 
facility cannot provide them.” Id. at para 58.

designed to recover the embedded costs of the existing grid, and that Constellation’s approach 
would shift grid costs onto others, or harm other customers by increasing transmission rates due 
to co-located data centers not paying their fair share for new transmission lines, substations, or 
voltage devices needed to maintain reliability, as well as network upgrades resulting from 
removing existing generation from the grid to serve a co-located load.12 Exelon argues that 
Constellation seeks a new service where there is no Network Customer, and thus no entity 
responsible for Commission-jurisdictional service charges.13 
Prior to the Constellation complaint, on November 1, 2024, the Commission convened a 
technical conference in Docket No. AD24-11-000 to examine issues related to large loads co-
located at generating facilities. Subsequently, the Commission issued the Show Cause Order, 
initiating a proceeding under section 206 of the Federal Power Act seeking answers from PJM, 
the Transmission Owners and the public regarding several relevant aspects of state and federal 
jurisdiction, transmission service, load and generation interconnection designs, resource 
adequacy, and cost allocation. 
III. 
COMMENTS AND REPLIES TO ORDER 
Throughout this inquiry and the preceding dockets, parties make arguments that begin with a 
presumption regarding the use of the transmission system by the co-located loads. The Show 
Cause Order includes briefing questions that explore the nature and implications of the 
transmission system use. In response to some of the briefing questions, we will document how 
the rapid changes in energy demand from data centers cause impacts on the transmission system. 
To mitigate these impacts, the connected utility system, (i.e. interconnected generators and the 
transmission system) requires ancillary services and transmission. 
 
12 Id. para 59. 
13 Id. para 61.

A. Transmission Service reliance 
  
Please explain whether and to what extent different configurations of co-located load rely 
on or otherwise use the transmission system to receive power, directly or indirectly, from the co-
located generator. 
UCS agrees with the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners that “all the arrangements 
being contemplated or requested as being interconnected with and synchronized with the 
transmission and/or distribution grid and thus not “fully isolated.”14 The co-located load, the co-
located generator and the transmission system are physically connected to allow power to flow 
continuously amongst them.15 Because there are recurring and unpredictable changes in the 
power flows to the co-located load, the proposed arrangements for co-located load are dependent 
on the transmission system to both receive power from the co-located generator and supply 
 
14 TO filing at page 9. 
15 Parties have described the load as “directly connected” to the co-located generator, which has 
an interconnection with the transmission system. See Complaint Requesting Fast Track 
Processing of Constellation Energy Generation, LLC. EL25-20 page 3-4. Included there is 
reference to Michael Kormos, The Co-Located Load Solution, (Nuclear Energy Inst. July 2024), 
which provides this illustration of connection between transmission, generation and co-located 
load.

power to the co-located load. The descriptions of the interaction between the load and the 
transmission system in the following paragraphs rely on observations by North American 
Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”), Electric Power Research Institute (“EPRI”), PJM, 
transmission owners, industry vendors, and researchers. 
 
NERC describes the simplest driver of varying power flows: the load’s consumption 
patterns differing from the generator’s production.16 In explicitly advising the Commission about 
reliability risks to the grid, NERC refers to circumstances when the co-located generation is not 
providing the same level of power as the co-located load is consuming.17 That is, when the co-
located load has demand which is greater than the output of the co-located generator, energy 
flows from the transmission system to the co-located load. When the co-located load is operating 
with energy demand less than the output of the co-located generator, energy flows from the 
generator to the transmission system. When the co-located load has demand that is the same as 
the production by the co-located generator, real energy does not flow to the transmission system. 
An illustration provided in comments shows power flows determined by the relative 
consumption and production of the facilities “behind a meter.” 18 
 
16 Howard Gugel. Statement of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation. 
Technical Conference on Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities Docket No. AD24-11-
000 November 1, 2024 
17 Id. “i.e., partial generation or no generation with the load connected.” 
18 See Response of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to the Order to Show Cause. See 
diagram created for two different hypothetical installations, which illustrate the power flows are

Broadly, the power sector operates within an environment of  routine patterns of power 
consumption changes across each hour and day, known as the “load ramp”. The “load ramp rate” 
is the change in power demand over time. The change in aggregated load on a utility system is 
mostly predictable, with patterns for the “morning ramp,” a peak in demand at the end of the day 
and a ramp down at night.19 Maintaining the balance between supply of electricity and demand 
for electricity is a central function for PJM20 and requires various responses drawing on the 
flexibility of supplies throughout a control area.21 When the load ramps at very high rate, or in 
unexpected ways, the challenges of matching of supply and demand become visible on the power 
system. 
 
determined by the relative size of the generator and the load at any moment in time.  
 
19  Energy Information Administration. “Demand for electricity changes through the day”  
https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=830 
20   PJM Operating Agreement  10.4 Duties and Responsibilities.  “Direct the operation and 
coordinate the maintenance of the facilities of the PJM Region used for both load and reactive 
supply, so as to maintain reliability of service and obtain the benefits of pooling and interchange 
consistent with this Agreement, and the Reliability Assurance Agreement.  
21 Id. Definitions. ““Control Area” shall mean an electric power system or combination of 
electric power systems bounded by interconnection metering and telemetry to which a common 
automatic generation control scheme is applied in order to: (a) match the power output of the 
generators within the electric power system(s) and energy purchased from entities outside the 
electric power system(s), with the load within the electric power system(s)… (d) maintain power 
flows on transmission facilities within appropriate limits to preserve reliability; and(e) provide 
sufficient generating capacity to maintain operating reserves in accordance with Good Utility 
Practice.”

EPRI reports that the utility industry has already seen variations in demand from existing 
data center operations affecting the power system. EPRI surveyed electric utilities about their 
experience serving data centers and EPRI reported utilities have already experienced operational 
impacts from connected data centers. The most common impact being reported is increased load 
ramp rates (26% of responding utilities).22 In addition, PJM uses the NERC Data Center Load 
Information Survey to assess data center load ramps.23 
 
The observation of data center load variability is widespread. PJM mentions them briefly. 
“These include unplanned generator run-backs or reductions in output, generator MW output 
oscillations, and co-located load utilization fluctuations. When these conditions occur, they result 
in brief, but routine, imbalances between the load and the generation that would need to rely on 
the grid to balance.”24 Reports from two regions with large amounts of data center load already 
connected to the power system, ERCOT25 and Virginia26, note substantial variability in demand 
in short time periods (e.g. less than one minute). These reports describe “imbalances between 
energy supply and demand [which] requires immediate action by our system operators.”27 
 
22 Utility Experiences and Trends Regarding Data Centers: 2024 Survey.  EPRI, Palo Alto, CA: 
2024. 3002030643. https://www.epri.com/research/products/000000003002030643  
23 Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Page 53. “Since 2024, PJM has been also collecting 
more granular data using the NERC Data Center Load Information Survey template to evaluate 
the impact of large data center co-located load ramping behaviors.  
24 Id. pages 44-45.  
25 ERCOT Stakeholder presentation - March 4, 2025. 
https://view.officeapps.live.com/op/view.aspx?src=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.ercot.com%2Ffiles
%2Fdocs%2F2025%2F02%2F28%2FLL-
Oscillation_LFLTF_Mar2025_Final.pptx&wdOrigin=BROWSELINK  
26 Pre-Technical Conference Statement of Kyle Hannah, Director of Electric Transmission 
Strategic Initiatives, Dominion Energy Inc. Docket  AD24-11-000 . 
27 Id.

The utility industry is only beginning to understand and categorize the variability of data 
center loads. At the same time, data centers’ energy use is increasing for processing larger and 
more complex individual tasks, increasing the amplitude of energy demand variations.28  
ERCOT’s recent discussion with stakeholders included a 300 MW drop in data center 
demand in 24 seconds, and oscillations of 25 MW repeatedly up and down in under one second, 
recurring again with 50 MW oscillations three days later.29 In academic and research efforts, 
measurements made inside computer facilities have provided illustrative measurements of data 
center demand ramping and oscillations when researchers examined behavior of various data 
processing tasks and tools.30,31  These researchers made direct measurements of energy demand 
patterns using varied software and computation instructions. The graphs below demonstrate high 
rates of change in electricity use while performing tasks, and the differences between earlier 
 
28 Forbes Business Insight. High Performance Computing Market Size, Growth Report [2032]. 
See also P. Patel, E. Choukse, C. Zhang, I. n. Goiri, B. Warrier, N. Mahalingam, and R. 
Bianchini, “Characterizing Power Management Opportunities for LLMs in the Cloud,” in 
Proceedings of the 29th ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for 
Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 3, ser. ASPLOS ’24, vol. 3. New York, 
NY, USA: Association for Computing Machinery, Apr. 2024, pp. 207–222. “In larger-scale 
training, such power swings are correlated across thousands of GPUs running the training job, 
which could cause challenges in the power delivery infrastructure.” 
29 ERCOT Stakeholder presentation  - March 4, 2025.

Workshops of The International Conference on High Performance Computing, Network, 
Storage, and Analysis, ser. SC-W ’23. New York, NY, USA: Association for Computing 
Machinery, Nov. 2023, pp. 1890–1893.  https://doi.org/10.1145/3624062.3624274 
31 Grant L. Stewart, Gregory A. Koenig, Jingjing Liu, Anders Clausen, Sonja Klingert, and 
Natalie Bates. 2019. “Grid Accommodation of Dynamic HPC Demand”. Workshop Proceedings 
of the 48th International Conference on Parallel Processing (ICPP Workshops '19). Association 
for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, Article 9, 1–4. 
https://doi.org/10.1145/3339186.3339214

workloads and now-common machine-learning computation.32 Note the steep ramp up in demand 
at the start of the tasks, followed by the oscillations such as were described by ERCOT, above. 
 
In recent information-sharing workshops, practitioners from industry have advised of 
“potential for forced oscillations in system due to periodic changes in active power” and “system 
voltage fluctuations is a concern if the load profile is variable”.33 Another spoke of active power 
changes in data center demand that can be expected to impact the required amount of automatic 
generator control, i.e. output from the generator supply.34 These sorts of load variability create 
 
32 Govind, S. Bhalachandra, Z. Zhao, E. Rrapaj, B. Austin, and H. A. Nam. 
33  Pooja Shah, Harish Sharma. Southern Company.  Interconnection and Integration of Large 
Loads ESIG Fall Workshop 2024,  slide 10. https://www.esig.energy/download/session-4a-
interconnection-and-integration-of-large-loads-pooja-shah-and-harish-
sharma/?wpdmdl=12221&refresh=671fa4964876b1730126998  
34 Julieta Giraldez, Ahmed Rashwan. Electric Power Engineers. Large Loads: Interconnection, 
Planning and Reliability Considerations. ESIG Fall Workshop 2024, slide 15.

imbalances more quickly than generators can correct, resulting in the voltage disturbances, 
thermal overloads and stability issues described by grid operators and NERC.35 The capability of 
individual generators to keep is measured in megawatts (MW) per minute, with steam units (coal 
or nuclear) in the range of 3-20 MW per minute at the slow end of the spectrum, and combustion 
turbines and pumped hydro capable of 50 MW per minute.36 The management of load ramp rates 
greater than the capability of single generators to match those ramps is achieved through 
ancillary services. 
 
B. Ancillary or other wholesale services reliance 
Please explain whether and to what extent different configurations of co-location 
arrangements rely on or benefit from ancillary services or black start services and, if so, provide 
specific details about the type of service and how the co-location arrangement relies on it. To 
what extent are these benefits distinct from the benefits that other Network Integration 
Transmission Service Point-to-Point Transmission Service customers derive from ancillary 
services? 
 
UCS agrees with PJM that “the load and generator are connected to and synchronized 
with the multi-state bulk power system. The load and generator are benefiting from ancillary 
services (including but not limited to black start).”37 The interaction between load, generation, 
and transmission in the connected and synchronized system involves a range of responses to 
maintain the balance between supply and demand that itself defines reliability.38 There are 
 
https://www.esig.energy/download/session-4a-large-loads-interconnection-planning-and-
reliability-considerations-julieta-giraldez-and-ahmed-
rashwan/?wpdmdl=12224&refresh=671fa495d3a361730126997  
35 Howard Gugel. Statement of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation. 
Technical Conference on Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities Docket No. AD24-11-
000 November 1, 2024. 
36   University of Wisconsin-Madison. Active Power Ramp Rates. 2013. https://neos-
guide.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/04/ramp_rates.pdf 
37 Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., page 42.

Wholesale Electricity Market Design with Increasing Levels of Renewable Generation National 
Renewable Energy Laboratory  NREL/TP-5D00-61765. 2014. “Three fundamental components 
comprise the wholesale electricity supply: generation, transmission, and coordination services.

numerous measurements of this balance over differing time horizons, and several ancillary 
services that define the cost of providing the service to maintain reliability.39 Further, these 
balancing services are distinct from the connection of the load and transport of energy to the load 
that occurs through the use of the transmission system. 
 
The above description of the variability of co-located loads and the mismatch with 
slower-ramping co-located generation forces the question of how this imposes costs for the 
ancillary services required to re-establish and maintain the balance and reliability of the system. 
In the technical conference proceeding, NERC noted the impact of data center energy 
consumption changing rapidly affecting “thermal overloads, voltage issues, or stability issues.”40 
Additional narrative from Dominion Energy41 describes the range of services maintaining 
reliability, serving differing time-frames and vulnerabilities of the electric power system 
“anytime a grid connection is maintained, even if reverse-power protection systems are in place 
to prevent the co-located load from drawing real power (MW) from the grid.”42 These numerous 
services stemming from system operation and securing reliability through scheduling and 
 
Each of these has a financial and physical component that must accommodate for the lack of a 
consumer response inherent to electricity markets while ensuring the constant balance of 
generation and load.” Page 4. 
39 See California ISO. https://www.caiso.com/market-operations/products-services/ancillary-
services  
40  Howard Gugel. Statement of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation. 
41 Pre-Technical Conference Statement of Kyle Hannah, Director of Electric Transmission 
Strategic Initiatives, Dominion Energy Inc. “Dominion Energy serves more data centers today 
than the next five domestic markets combined.” 
42 Id. “Both the load and generator benefit from the essential reliability services provided by the 
transmission grid. These benefits include load balancing, primary frequency response, reactive 
compensation, voltage control, short-circuit fault current, and system inertia. Essential reliability 
services are provided anytime a grid connection is maintained, even if reverse-power protection 
systems are in place to prevent the co-located load from drawing real power (MW) from the 
grid.”

dispatching of generation resources43 are ancillary services separate from transmission service. 
The variable co-located loads rely on both the transmissions system to deliver the ancillary 
services and those ancillary services to mitigate the impacts to the transmission system caused by 
that co-located load. 
C.    Transmission Service Requirements 
Please explain whether co-location arrangements are or should be required to take 
Network Integration Transmission Service or Point-to-Point Transmission Service; or whether a 
more tailored new category of transmission service is warranted. 
  
Co-location arrangements should be required to take either Network Integration 
Transmission Service or Point-to-Point Transmission Service. The existing terms and conditions 
of these services are sufficient.  As noted in the Show Cause Order, the Commission has defined 
transmission service as the provision of “electric transmission, network or point-to-point service, 
ancillary services or other methods of electric transmission, or the interconnection with 
jurisdictional transmission facilities.”44 The co-location arrangements all include one or more 
pieces of equipment (conductors, breakers, and or substations) between the co-located load and 
the co-located generator. 45 These are attached to the generator’s own Interconnection Facilities 
(specifically the Interconnection Customer’s Interconnection Facilities) which are 
jurisdictional.46 By the definition cited, there is Commission-defined transmission service 
separate and prior to the initiation of operations and the variable flow of energy to serve the load. 
 
Once the co-located load begins to operate, the varying consumption described above is a 
 
43 See PJM Operating Agreement, Schedule 1, Section 1.6.  
44 Show Cause Order para 76. 
45   Affidavit of Steven R. Herling. October 2, 2024. Docket Nos. ER24-2888-000, ER24-2889-
000, ER24-2890-000. Page 5. 
46 LGIA 5.10 “Interconnection Customer's Interconnection Facilities ('ICIF'). Interconnection 
Customer shall, at its expense, design, procure, construct, own and install the ICIF.”

factor affecting PJM’s transmission capacity for errors in short-term load forecasting.  PJM must 
maintain a margin of transmission capacity separate from providing reserves in generation to 
meet supply shortfalls. PJM, as the Transmission Provider and Transmission Operator, calculates 
available transmission capacity with a reserve known as the Transmission Reliability Margin 
which is set “to represent historical load forecast error” in the day-ahead time horizon. 47 In this 
way, PJM uses the transmission system to manage reliability impacts from unforeseen changes in 
load. New variability in the load not previously included in calculating this margin will quite 
possibly require new Transmission Reliability Margin levels in some or all of PJM. 
IV. 
Conclusion 
In these comments we explain what it means to be “electrically connected and synchronized 
to the PJM Transmission System when consuming power” and how that implicates the use of 
both ancillary services and transmission service. We illustrate how the fully isolated load idea is 
a fiction, supported only by a private contract that does not establish different physical facts. The 
loads require transmission and ancillary services because the host generators are unable to 
operate without the grid. The host generators are unable to provide all the required capabilities to   
match the variable load. There is evidence enough to conclude there are no fully isolated loads in 
these cases of existing generators proposals. “In order for a co-location arrangement (i.e., the 
generator plus data center) to obtain these services, the grid itself must exist. Ancillary services 
pass through transmission lines, not the air.”48 
 
47 PJM Transmission Reliability Margin TRM Implementation Document. “PJM includes TRM 
in the AFC/ATC process to provide a reasonable level of assurance that the interconnected 
transmission network will be secure. PJM applies a default value of 2% of the flowgate rating to 
represent historical load forecast error.” 
https://connect.pjm.com/sites/ftp/ftppjmcom/oasis/TRMID.pdf  
48 Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. page 36

Respectfully submitted on this 10th day of April 2025.
